summary:
This is a geospatial monitoring platform designed to assess post-wildfire landscape changes and identify watersheds that may require closer environmental monitoring. Using the 2026 Timber and Plaskett fire areas in Big Sur, California, the project analyses satellite observations across separate fire-specific timelines.

The current optical workflow uses Sentinel-2 imagery to calculate pre-fire and post-fire Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) and differenced NBR (dNBR), identifying areas with significant spectral changes. It combines these results with NASA SRTM elevation data, terrain slope and USGS HUC-12 watershed boundaries to examine how landscape changes relate to watershed characteristics.

The project is designed to extend this assessment using NISAR L-band radar observations, allowing optical and radar-based changes to be compared. Its dashboard brings satellite maps, fire-wise statistics, terrain information and watershed monitoring priorities into one interface.

The goal is to make post-fire landscape assessment more accessible and help guide targeted environmental monitoring, rather than claim to predict disasters.
details:
Project Details: AETHERIX

Project Overview

Wildfires do not stop affecting the environment when the flames disappear. Their consequences can continue long after containment, causing vegetation loss, exposing soil, altering surface conditions and potentially increasing the vulnerability of downstream watersheds. However, post-wildfire assessments often focus primarily on mapping burned areas, leaving an important question unanswered: Where should environmental monitoring be prioritised after a wildfire, and why?

AETHERIX is an interactive geospatial platform designed to address this challenge. It analyses post-wildfire landscape changes and connects satellite observations with terrain characteristics and watershed conditions to identify areas that may require closer environmental monitoring. Our case study focuses on the 2026 Timber and Plaskett fires in Big Sur, California.

How It Works

AETHERIX combines satellite observations, terrain information and watershed boundaries through an integrated geospatial workflow.

1. Satellite-Based Change Detection

We use Sentinel-2 Level-2A imagery to examine pre-fire and post-fire conditions. By calculating the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR) and differenced NBR (dNBR), the platform identifies areas showing significant vegetation and surface changes. Cloud masking, temporal filtering and image compositing help prepare the observations for analysis.

2. Terrain and Watershed Analysis

NASA SRTM elevation data, terrain slope and USGS HUC-12 watershed boundaries are incorporated to understand how observed landscape changes are distributed across watersheds. This provides geographical context for assessing potentially vulnerable areas.

3. Multi-Sensor Earth Observation

AETHERIX is designed to incorporate NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar observations alongside Sentinel-2 optical imagery. Radar can provide observations through cloud cover and responds to surface properties differently from optical sensors. Combining these complementary observations offers an opportunity to investigate changes that may not be fully captured by optical imagery alone.

4. Watershed Monitoring Prioritisation

The platform combines landscape-change indicators and terrain characteristics to develop a relative monitoring priority assessment for affected watersheds. Instead of treating every location equally, it helps highlight areas that may deserve further investigation.

5. Interactive Dashboard

All analytical outputs are presented through an interactive dashboard featuring fire boundaries, satellite imagery, pre-fire and post-fire comparisons, change-detection maps, terrain layers, watershed-level statistics and monitoring priorities. Users can explore individual fires and watersheds to understand the spatial distribution of observed changes.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Moves beyond conventional burned-area mapping to examine post-fire landscape changes.
  • Helps identify watersheds that may require closer environmental monitoring.
  • Connects satellite observations with terrain and watershed characteristics.
  • Makes complex Earth-observation information accessible through interactive visualisations.
  • Provides a potentially scalable workflow for assessing other wildfire-affected regions.

Our goal is to support more informed post-wildfire environmental monitoring by helping researchers and environmental decision-makers understand not only where a wildfire occurred, but also where its consequences deserve further investigation.

Technology and Tools

  • Google Earth Engine: Satellite data access, cloud masking, image compositing and geospatial analysis.
  • Sentinel-2: Optical imagery for NBR and dNBR change detection.
  • NASA SRTM: Elevation data for terrain analysis.
  • USGS HUC-12: Watershed boundaries and watershed-level assessment.
  • QGIS: Geospatial processing, inspection and visualisation.
  • Web technologies: Interactive dashboard development and geospatial visualisation.
  • NASA-ISRO NISAR: Planned integration of L-band radar observations.

Creativity and Innovation

The key innovation of AETHERIX is its focus on connecting post-fire landscape changes with watershed-level monitoring priorities. Rather than presenting satellite images as isolated observations, it brings together different environmental datasets to provide a more meaningful picture of the affected landscape.

Its multi-sensor research direction, combining optical observations with NISAR radar, further explores whether complementary satellite technologies can improve post-wildfire landscape assessment.

Factors Considered

The workflow considers fire-specific timelines, satellite acquisition dates, cloud contamination, image quality, spatial resolution, seasonal vegetation changes, surface moisture, terrain variability and watershed boundaries. Monitoring priorities are treated as relative screening indicators, not as predictions of debris flows or substitutes for field validation.

AETHERIX aims to turn Earth-observation data into actionable environmental insights, helping make post-wildfire monitoring more targeted, informed and accessible.
